utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have our witness brought in, please, that is, General Blaskic. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters and to the court reporters. Good morning to the Defence and to the Prosecution counsel and to the witness. If everybody can hear me, and I hope everybody can, we can continue. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps this is a good point to introduce the photographs, the still photographs, which were taken yesterday. We only have a single colour series, and the rest of them are black and white. Perhaps we could also place them on the ELMO and ask General Blaskic to just quickly describe each one of them and then have each one assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As regards the photographs, this will be D542/1-7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first photograph is D542/1. Could you just briefly describe this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe you said you had black and white copies if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The quality is very poor, so you can barely see it. What we need to do is we need to have additional copies made for the rest of the parties. We tried to make them, but we were unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a problem for you, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. It's easier, of course, to make notes on a particular document as the witness is talking about it so, of course, at the appropriate time, we would like that because it would be very useful in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. I have another request. I would like this, and I have already said it, I frequently say it, that when documents are put on the ELMO, the public gallery should be able to see them as well. These are public hearings, let me remind you. We have enough closed hearings for other reasons, and so I would like to remind you of that. I know that technically it's a bit complicated, but I'm supervising the matter because I can see that we have people in the public gallery. These are public hearings, let me remind you of that, unless, of course, we come to a different decision. All right. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you please describe what the photograph D542/1 represents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph represents the checkpoints which were established starting on 2nd January, 1993 until 20th January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: By the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The position I am pointing at is Vitez (indicating). This is Travnik (indicating). This is Novi Travnik (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just briefly, these are the BH army checkpoints in Vitez, Novi Travnik, and Travnik in January 1993; can we define them like that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next photograph, please, D545/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like for the witness to define, very quickly, not to go over what we went over yesterday, so the witness sees the photos, sees the legend, the legend is written and registered with the registry. Please go on, Witness. We don't want to waste any time. Please go forward. Please go ahead. We have the description. Read the description and then go on to the next.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This photograph shows the checkpoints in the Travnik municipality, deployment of the HVO forces and the forces of the BH army against the front line with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Next photograph, D542/3.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This photograph shows the checkpoint established near the Vodovod elementary school by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the checkpoint is designated by the yellow piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Next photograph, D542/4.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The photograph shows the checkpoint of the BH army in Kruscica, and it is designated in yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Next photograph, D542/5.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The photograph shows the checkpoints set up by the BH army on the main road Novi Travnik-Gornji Vakuf. The yellow markers mark the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Next photograph, D542/6.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The photograph shows checkpoints set up by the BH army from Kacuni to Bilalovac. The yellow markers mark the checkpoints themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. The next photograph, the last photograph, D542/7.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is the same photograph. This shows the situation of January 1993 and shows the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean the checkpoints between Kacuni and Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, between Kacuni and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. So we left off yesterday, at the end of the day, at 25 January, 1993 when, in the afternoon, you received information about fighting in Busovaca. What exactly did you receive in terms of information, and did you receive sufficient information in order to be able to start to exercise your command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: During that day, I received information that a conflict had broken out at the checkpoint at Kacuni where a member of the HVO military police was killed and another civilian, who could not be identified at the moment, and the rest of the information was pretty scant, and they did not allow me to get the full picture of what was going on in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown Exhibits D95, 96, and 406. If this is D95, can you put it on the ELMO, the English version, please? First, D95, please, and apparently there's no English translation right now, so I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is to the 4th Military Police Battalion, 4th Military Police Battalion, and then the registration number is there. The date is 25 January, 1993, and it says: "To the Command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone (Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, Kiseljak)." The heading is "Report." "On 25 January, 1993 around 0100 hours in the village of Kacuni, in the fighting between the members of the HVO units in Busovaca and the BH army, Ivica Petrovic, member of the Busovaca HVO, and an unknown person, whose identity has not yet been established, were killed. The on-site investigation of this incident was conducted by the crime department with the Mostar/Vitez HVO department," and it is signed by Pasko Ljubicic, the commander. General Blaskic, did you receive this report such as we see here?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received it on the 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In what fashion did you receive it, by what means?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I think that the report was received by fax, I think through the local telephone lines between Kiseljak and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, what were the telephone lines like in the Busovaca, Vitez, and Kiseljak area? What lines were used? What cables were used? Where were the cables passing through?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The cables themselves were between Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, and they went through Kacuni and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In such circumstances, could you use the regular civilian telephone lines for military command and control and for reception of the military reports?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, because we had certain knowledge that these lines were not safe, that they were monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to Exhibit D96. This is an order which was not confirmed, has not been authenticated, by any witness so far, as I'm being signalled by the registrar, so we have no translation, so I'm going to read it. It states: "Command post of OZ SB, forward command post in Vitez." The number is SB1881/93, and the date is the 25th of January, 1993, and it says, "Deliver to the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca directly," and the heading is "Assignment of Persons for the Joint Commission," and it says, "Pursuant to the proposal delivered by the commander of the 3rd Army Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina," the number "02/33-320 of 25 January, 1993, point 5," and the response sent, "number 02/33-327 of 25 January, 1993, point 3, by the 3rd Corps of the BH army, I order the following: "The commander of the HVO brigade Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca will appoint a person who will establish the telephone contact and be authorised to adopt any decisions in the zone of responsibility of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca. 2. The basic role of the commission is to work on tasks of immediate cease-fire between the HVO and the BH army. 3. Members of the commission should be selected based on the assessment and proposals of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade command. 4. The deadline for carrying out of this order is 25 January 1993, 1500 hours." It is signed by the Commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. First, can you tell me, did you write this order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, let us analyse it a little bit. It contains several slightly illogical points, including the Croatian language. First of all, let's look at the registration number. Is this the registration number used by the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who could it have been used by?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was in Kiseljak that day, and as I did not have the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command logbook in order to assign a proper registration number, so through the packet communications, I asked from my staff to register this order, that is, this staff to assign it a number, which it decides. So where it says "S.B.", it should have stated "T.B.", that means "Tihomir Blaskic," and these were the numbers in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. We're moving on to the preamble. It looks from it as if the letter of the 3rd Corps has a registration number of the 3rd Corps, and it looks as if your response also has the 3rd Corps registration number. Is this a mistake, or what is this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is probably a mistake because the operative who probably typed up this document, and this document was sent via packet communications, probably was not able to read my handwriting because my order was written by hand, and I believe that I was probably sending it to the 3rd Corps, and the 3rd Corps was responding to me; in other words, I communicated with Enver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So do you agree that this preamble is not logical and that some mistakes and errors are involved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next question is: Why are you not assigning the person to negotiate but you are giving this authority to the Busovaca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was not in full control of the situation and I did not have full information about what was going on in Busovaca, and the commander of the brigade, I was not sure whether he was able to return from Zepce. This was Mr. Niko Juzinovic. I still believed at that time that this was an incident in Kacuni and that the conflict did not spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Could Exhibit D406 be placed on the ELMO, and here we do have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this, it says the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command, and the number is 01-1-366/93, dated the 26th of January, 1993, and the time is 2300 hours. It is addressed to the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, in Kiseljak. If you look at the signature, it is the chief of staff, Franjo Nakic. Could you first, please, just review the document, and then say how it was delivered to you? Please, the back page also.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This document was faxed to me using the regular civilian telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're not going to read the entire document. Just point 2, which talks about the communications. "1. Report on the sending of wires by packet communications - packet communications of the main staff of the HVO are not fully operational (only the participants from Herzegovina can receive them). - there is a need for checking identification documents due to a frequent appearance of foreigners (Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina). - there is a high overload of the entire packet network in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. - there is a high frequency of packet network interceptions - within the Central Bosnia Operative Zone packet network, only the Vitez network is operational at the moment, Travnik and Novi Travnik packets have limited capacity, the Kiseljak packet operates exclusively through Vitez, Zenica and Busovaca packets are not operating within the network but only by using a special frequency with Vitez, which creates the additional difficulties of operating on two frequencies; the Zepce packet is entirely out of use. - operators in the Kiseljak packet communications cannot operate full-time, and they neither have the training nor the equipment to use this frequency. - BH Army participants have already attempted to intercept our wires, which has been noticed by the packet of the main staff of the HVO; we are therefore forced to run maximum checks on every participant." I'm not going to read the rest of the document, but I want to ask you: Did you actually receive this fax in Kiseljak from your command post in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you very briefly, just a couple of sentences, explain what the packet communication system was which you used and which you used in addition to the civilian lines, and was there a third system which you used?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have any additional communication systems. The packet communications, as described, was the only communication means we had, and what happened was we used one telephone line and modem on the computer through which messages were sent. The operator would type up the text and then send to the addressee this typewritten text. However, the security problems with the packet communication lines were very high because any operator could send a message and any operator could receive it; they only needed to know the code.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You said that you used a modem and used the telephone line. Do you mean telephone line or the radio line?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Radio line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you misspoke just now.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell me what problems were involved in sending a message in this way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The biggest problems were to secure this message; in other words, other participants in this communication traffic were able to receive such messages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you will kindly bear with the Bench. We know that all the witnesses have used the term "packet communication," and no doubt it has been explained here and there. But this is such a significant witness. I wonder whether you would think it useful to ask him to explain very neatly and concisely what the reference means?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, would you, in the briefest of terms, explain the technicalities of that link and the communications you used? What devices were used and what was the idea?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We used ordinary computers that we had in the economy. They were not specific, special military computers, they were ordinary computers, the kind that you could buy on the market, business computers, and we used the existing lines that the PTT use, the Post, Telegraph, and Telephone service used, but we would use radio relay stations and an adapter or modem which we used, we used this additional modem which enabled communication between the users in this packet communication link network.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How would a text be sent? Could you explain the procedure to us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: When I wrote an order or a document, if it was urgent, then I could hand it to the operator who was at the computer, and the operator would then type out the order on the computer. After that, he would call the next user in the communication line, that is to say, a neighbouring computer to which the text was addressed, and if communication between the two computers existed, then the text would be sent on to the next user or the next participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you use a computer and a modem; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the message is on the air waves, radio waves, where does the problem lie? Must it reach the receiver, the person receiving the message, or can somebody intercept the message?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These are two problems which were serious ones, and one problem was that if somebody knew the code of the participant, then this message could be taken over and intercepted by anybody who knew the code. The other problem was that if somebody else wanted to interfere with the packet link, then they would be able to send a message themselves. For example, if I were sending a message from Kiseljak and the 3rd Corps was aware of the code, it too can send from the communications centre a message to the command of the Operative Zone in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it a code or was it a question of knowing the frequency you were using?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Those are two matters. Frequency is one thing. If you know the frequency, you can take part in the communication itself, but the participants had their own codes and code names. For example, they had a very simple code name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So they identified themselves by stating a name; can we put it in layman's terms in that way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, could you wrap it up by explaining to us whether there could be any interception if you applied the packet method of communication which, as you have explained to us, means really communication from computer to computer? Could there be any interception if that method were used?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, especially as we had just started using this method and had no protective devices, and I tried to explain this a moment ago. Interception was possible, both with the conveyance of the message, but what could also be done was that another message could be sent under a false name or code.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it could be a false order, in fact; is that right? A false order could be introduced?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, getting back to the very beginning of the conflict in which you were allied with the 3rd Corps, or you were dealing with the 3rd Corps, now we're dealing with various means that were used for communications and for other logistics. So in the very beginning, did this pose any more important problems?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did have cooperation in the sense that the heads of communications took part; for example, my own and Enver's would have meetings, and they would settle those technical details. I don't know how they actually did this, I don't know the details in the technical sense, but as I say, there were difficulties because at that time we were allies, we were truly and genuinely allies, and we had a whole link-up system of communications, so there were no secrets. The head of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone would be sitting down together.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, General, if you would?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can therefore deduce that you yourself were able to intercept communications from the 3rd Corps, for example?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, yes. The difference being that, Your Honours, the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina inherited the communication system from the zone headquarters of the Territorial Defence of Zenica, and I'm talking about the time when the JNA was stationed in Zenica itself, and I mean the Territorial Defence as a component of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia. So they inherited the communications and link system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And that communication system, in the technical sense, at what level was it compared to your own communication system?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: For all intents and purposes, that system of communications enabled operative command to take place whereas the system of links and communications that we're talking about in the HVO was a system that was under formation, it was a fledgling system of packet communications, if you like, and not all the operators had been trained yet sufficiently to work with those systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, according to your experience -- you are not a specialist in communications -- but this system of packet links and communications that you used, is it a professional military system which enabled operative command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was not a professional military system because operative command implies command in real time and real space whereas, according to the documents, we can see that some of the documents travelled from Kiseljak to Vitez as long as two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Explain to the Trial Chamber -- and I think this is an important point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General Blaskic. We know that beyond your own professional military training, you also have computer training. Did this computer training that you received aid you in installing or in improving the communications in that situation or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, had I had the cadres and the resources, that knowledge would have helped me. Let me quote an example. The head of communications for the Operative Zone and my headquarters had secondary education, vocational training, he was a radio technician, and he had worked in the Maintenance Institute of Travnik and was trained to maintain radios; but to command and control devices and units, that was something that he did not know about at the time, and I didn't have anybody else working with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The software that you used in the computers, was it a special type of software devised for the purposes and needs of the army, or was it something that could be purchased in any computer shop?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was not any kind of military software, no. As far as I know, it was the usual type of business software that could be bought on the market, in shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned a term a moment ago which I think deserves the Court's attention, "command in real time." What does "real time" mean in military terms?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, we mentioned informatics and computers and how this helped, and the term that I was acquainted with in the former Yugoslav People's Army, that term implied that the military commander receives information at the time when the event actually takes place in a certain region and that he has the possibility of reacting and influencing and guiding the course of events. That is to say, to react simultaneously upon the reception of that information. Today, in addition to commanding in real space and communication and control, there is also a selective approach to the multitude of information which is sent at all times to the commanding officer, and all this with the aim of enabling him to react as speedily as possible and exert influence on the events in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We looked at D96, the previous document, it was written on the 25th of January, 1993, and the stamp was the radio packet dated the 27th of January, 1993. It was probably at 4.00 a.m., 4.00 in the morning. Tell us, please, is this an example of the level of communication that you had at the time, and what did this kind of information mean to you as a commander, information that was sent to you five or six hour later or a day and a half later? How did this influence the possibility of reacting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is just one example. There were quite definitely many examples of this kind. This kind of information sent in this way and received in this way made it impossible for the receiver, in this case, it was the command in Vitez, to react on time, to have a timely reaction, because two days elapsed before this information reached the commander, and so you cannot really react properly. If information is as late as this, it is impossible to command in terms of real time and real space.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. This brings us to the 26th of January. You are still in Kiseljak cut off from the events in Busovaca, and you have a meeting at 10.00 a.m. with Dzemo Merdan and General Cordy-Simpson. Can you tell us how this meeting came about and what you discussed at the meeting and what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The meeting of the 26th of January, 1993 at around 10.00 a.m. at the headquarters of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina was held. Mr. Cordy-Simpson and Colonel Bob Stewart were present, Dzemo Merdan was present from the 3rd Corps, and I, myself, attended the meeting. The meeting was convened on the basis of a request from myself made on the 25th of January and at the demand of UNPROFOR, that we should have a meeting and agree upon a cease-fire, a cessation of the conflicts with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I, first of all, requested a cessation of the conflict. That was my first request. Second, I demanded that the barricades at Kacuni be dismantled and that the road be opened running from Kiseljak and Busovaca, that there be free passage along that road, and I also requested a complete freedom of movement along the Kiseljak-Busovaca road. Dzemo Merdan did not contest the fact that the conflict should be stopped. The point that was contested had to do with the troops from outside, that is to say, the engagement of forces outside the municipality of Busovaca in this conflict. Nonetheless, in the course of the meeting, we succeeded in agreeing on practically all the points that we discussed, and at one particular moment during the meeting, a message reached me, it was brought to me in the hall where we were having our meeting, which said that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been launching combat operations in the Lasva, Dusina, and Visnjica area and that the Croatian civilians in those villages had been slaughtered. I reacted in the following fashion: I asked Dzemo to have these operations stopped, and I told him that we could not sit down and discuss things of this kind while the 3rd Corps was launching these attacks, and that particular meeting was interrupted temporarily, and it ended by us having reached an agreement that on the next day at 10.00 a.m., that is to say, on the 27th of January, 1993, we would meet again at the same venue and that that meeting would be attended by the commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver, who had usually come to meetings of this kind with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, did Dzemo Merdan promise to see what was happening in Lasva and Dusina and that he would stop the killing of civilians there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that at that particular point, from the venue of the meeting, he did not have any communications, and he was not able to ascertain what was going on and that the best thing would be if he personally were to investigate and see what was going on in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now move on to another meeting that was held, but I just remembered one point and that is to ask you the following: Did you have or did the 3rd Corps have brigade vehicles and centres, that is to say, mobile communication centres, on the basis of which the commander could command combat activities wherever he was located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We called them the radio relay system of communications and links for the level of the brigade of the former JNA, whereas in the HVO, we did not have a single system of that kind. We did not have them in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and I know for a fact that, from the technical maintenance institute of Travnik, systems of this kind were taken over by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the following day, that is to say, the 27th of January, 1993, at the headquarters of the United Nations in Kiseljak, at 10.00 a.m., another meeting was held at which Enver Hadzihasanovic turned up. The commander of the 3rd Corps had entered that meeting. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how that meeting evolved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Enver Hadzihasanovic from the 3rd Corps came to attend the meeting, but Kadir Jusic from the 3rd Corps also came to the meeting. He came from Visoko. The meeting was also attended by the head of the European Monitoring Mission, Mr. Flemming. At the very start of the meeting, Enver made the observation that I was isolated, that I was cut off in Kiseljak and that, quite obviously, the HVO in the Lasva River Valley was being commanded by somebody else. He agreed to have the meeting start only when I had given him assurances as to who the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone actually was, and I confirmed that it is quite true that I was in Kiseljak, but that as far as I knew, I, myself, was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you able to confirm and actually tell him that you were not in control of the events in Busovaca as a commander should be?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, at that particular moment, it was a meeting between us, the conflicting parties, and, of course, I did not own up to this. I did not affirm this because my positions were anyway subordinated under conditions of that kind, inferior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we now show the witness Defence Exhibit D128. Defence Exhibit 188. Please, the English transcript on the ELMO, the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read from this document D188 only three items, and this is a report of Enver Hadzihasanovic to the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The top of the third paragraph: "We assume that Colonel Tihomir Blaskic is isolated in Kiseljak and that his readiness to solve the problems is a lie, that somebody else is solving the problems instead of Tiho Blaskic, and that there is no point in negotiating as whatever is agreed upon will not have any result," and the last sentence, "The HVO main headquarters would need to be asked to designate a person other than Colonel Blaskic, which would be," and I can't read it very well, "which would have the authority to take decisions," and then Enver Hadzihasanovic signed this. This is a document which, obviously, you could not have seen because this is Hadzihasanovic's report, and this is an opinion expressed by him to his supreme command. Does this coincide with his position which he orally expressed to you on that occasion during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After you tried to sort of salvage your position, did the meeting continue, and what was the outcome of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The negotiations were continued. The basic issue that we discussed was the cease-fire, which is what I requested, and withdrawal of troops outside of the Busovaca municipality, that is, of the troops which took part in this conflict. I tried the clearing of the battleground, the opening up of the road at Kacuni, and the return of the entire situation to the condition as of 23 January, 1993, and we managed to agree in this meeting, to come to this agreement, on the cease-fire. We signed the agreement and presented it publicly before the media, and the host during this meeting and the mediator was Brigadier Cordy-Simpson in Kiseljak. After the meeting, I went to the Kiseljak barracks, and I worked on a draft of a document on the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can I now please ask that document D348 be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is document D348 from 27 January, 1993. You sent it to the head of the defence department in Mostar and to all the brigades and independent units. The title is "Implementation of the agreement of the cease-fire," and I'll just read a few paragraphs. "1. Implement the cease-fire, including all the parties. Enable the UNPROFOR monitors to monitor the cease-fire. Allow free passage of all vehicles of the personnel of UNPROFOR and the UNHCR and other humanitarian organisations," and then also, "Enable the exchange of prisoners through the auspices of the Red Cross." You also are trying to identify the person who was going to the joint commission, et cetera, et cetera. Is this a document that was drafted on the basis of the meeting which you had?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The points of the agreement are pretty much identical with the points in this order, and this order was issued out of the meeting held with the commander of the 3rd Corps in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 27th of January, after this meeting, you received first news about violence in the Croatian villages of Nezirovici, Besici, Gusti Grab, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received this information after the meeting, and I believe that this was late at night, that in the course of the day, the units of the 3rd Corps had attacked the Croatian villages of Nezirovici, Besici, Prosje and that these villages were taken by the BH army and that the civilians were driven out from these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you point out those villages on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The attack took place on the same day of the meeting, General Blaskic, these attacks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The same day as the meeting you had with UNPROFOR and General Cordy-Simpson; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and with your permission, I can show on the model where this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps use the model since we have it handy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you wish to approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is the village of Nezirovici (indicating) that was attacked on that day, that is, on the 27th of January, 1993, and Croats from this village were driven out towards Oseliste and Gusti Grab, that is, in the direction of Kiseljak. Here is the village of Besici, which is also a Croatian village, and Croats were driven out towards Oseliste, and Prosje is in this location. It may be better to show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, I think that this is enough. We're aware of the general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I have some difficulty in seeing it. I think that the map gives an idea of the geography, especially the orientation. So from which direction did they come? Where is Kiseljak, first of all?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is Kiseljak (indicating). This is the main road leading to Busovaca (indicating). On the 27th, we held a meeting here (indicating), and the villages that were attacked are Nezirovici, which I'm pointing at now (indicating), then the village of Besici, and the village of Prosje, in which that day, during the attack, a chapel was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you say who attacked these Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was the forces of the 3rd Army Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They drove out the Croats from these villages in the direction of Oseliste and Gusti Grab.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Later on, we will see what happened to Oseliste and Gusti Grab which was ethnically cleansed of Croats, but now I would like to show you a document which speaks to the first crime that took place in the Lasva Valley, the first crime against civilians, and this is Exhibit D434. The Jure Francetic HVO Brigade from Zenica sent this document on the 27th of January, 1993, but it was only received on the 29th of January, 1993, and the heading is "Report on the Massacre of Croats in the Village of Dusina, Lasva Local Commune." "On 27 January, 1993, displaced persons from the village of Dusina, Lasva local commune, arrived in Zenica and informed us of the massacre of Croats in the above-mentioned area. "Early on the morning of 26 January 1993, the Muslim Liberation Forces or MOS from Zenica surrounded seven Croatian houses in the village of Dusina. They demanded that the Dusina HVO members surrender their weapons. After it was agreed that the demand would be honoured, MOS members opened fire on the Croatian houses. The shooting claimed the lives of the following individuals: 1. Pero Rajic ... 2. Drazenko Kegelj ... 3. Frano Rajic ..." And then, in brackets, their fathers' names. "Zvonko Rajic ... was killed during the negotiations. The following two individuals were wounded: 1. Marko Rajic ... 2. Blasko Bosnjak ... The wounded were transported to the Zenica hospital. After the shooting ceased, MOS members entered the village, closed the civilians in the house owned by Stipe Kegelj ... and kept him there until the night. The HVO soldiers were arrested and their weapons were seized. After that, they started searching houses, threatening to shoot those who refused to surrender their weapons, because they had been informed by --" and this note, it's barely legible, it's probably "local Muslims" -- "that there were additional weapons. As they were unable to find more weapons, they carried out executions. The following people were executed: 1. Niko Kegelj ... 2. Vinko Kegelj ... 3. Jozo Kegelj ... 4. Mladenko Kegelj ... 5. August Rados ... After the execution, the soldiers' bodies were taken to a cellar in a family house ..." And then it says Marinko Kegelj managed to escape, and his father, Stipo Kegelj, was executed instead. "The following people are missing and their whereabouts are unknown: 1. Perica Rados ... 2. Dragan Rados ... 3. Nedjeljko Rajic ... 4. Marinko Kegelj ... After having executed the HVO soldiers, MOS members wanted to shoot Zdravka Rados, Dragan Rados's wife. It is assumed that they abandoned their idea to carry out the execution at the request of a local Muslim." And so on and so forth. Commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, Zivko Totic. Did this information reach you somehow in Kiseljak in the course of January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This information on the incidents in these villages reached me as early as 26 January on a -- I received it on a piece of paper, that is, that the attack was in progress during this meeting which I had with Dzemo Merdan. He saw this piece of paper, as did the other participants in the meeting, but not in this form, only that the attack was under way and that the Kegelj family was executed, but who it was specifically that was -- how many members were executed, that I did not know. Only late in January, I believe this was probably on the 30th or 31st of January, I received this information that you see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said that on the 27th you received information about Croats being driven out of their villages to Gusti Grab, Besici, and Nezirovici, and on the 29th of January, 1993, in the Muslim media, the Muslim media have announced their entry in Busovaca. Did you receive that information in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had already talked about it in Kiseljak, and through Radio Visoko and other media, it was announced that the only thing remaining was the entry in Busovaca, that all the other positions had been taken by the BH army and that they expected them to move into Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a good time to suspend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Twenty minutes' recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. We are now resuming with the examination-in-chief. I apologise for this delay. Of course, this was not intentional. Let us now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the break, we were talking about the 29th of January when the media announced the fall of Busovaca. You were in Kiseljak. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We received this information, as I have already said, via the media, that Busovaca was just about to fall and that, in the course of the day, the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were expected to enter Busovaca, and that in the afternoon, Busovaca would be liberated. After that, we received information in Kiseljak, that is to say, it was a request to extend aid and assistance to the population of Gusti Grab, a village in the Busovaca area, and that the wounded should be evacuated from the villages of Sirovi Panj, Oseliste, and Gusti Grab, that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you undertook and what happened, and could you just point the places out to us on the model?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe you can move the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The events that we're going to talk about occurred in the immediate vicinity of this barricade, the barricade was at Oseliste, and it was locally referred to as Donji Bukovac, the villagers called it Donji Bukovac, and it was on the main road from Busovaca to Kiseljak. On the map ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, are we now looking at the consequences of the fall of Busovaca; is that correct? Is that what you're asking the witness now? I want to make sure that I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. The media, the Muslim media, had announced that Busovaca would be falling on that day, but Busovaca had not fallen. On the road between Kiseljak and Busovaca, there were several Croatian villages which were still under attack, and the witness is now going to recount what happened in those villages on the road between Kiseljak and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps one sentence would be enough, would suffice. On the 27th, there was an attack on Nezirovici and Besici, the villages I mentioned, and the Croats from the Nezirovici village and Besici --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you slow down, please, General, for the benefit of the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: After an attack by the BH army, they withdrew --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea to bring the microphone up closer, it is too far away at the moment, because the interpreters can't hear you properly. Try and slow down, please, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, when the witness moves about, I would like for the court usher to be next to the witness to try to help him so that we do not lose any more time. Sir, would you please try to do that? We always have problems in the movement. It would make things much easier if we would have the usher on hand to intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: From the villages of Nezirovici and Besici, the Croats were expelled on the 27th of January, 1993, after the attack launched by the forces of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 29th of January, 1993, the expulsed Croats from Nezirovici and Besici found themselves in the area of Oseliste, it is marked on the map, and I received a request from Busovaca, from the HVO in Busovaca openly, by phone, in Kiseljak to extend assistance in taking in the refugee Croats from Gusti Grab and Oseliste, to take them in and to evacuate the wounded from that area. In the morning, we sent a first aid vehicle, ambulance, to evacuate the wounded, and at the checkpoint at Donji Bukovci, and the exact position of that checkpoint is the one I am indicating at present (indicating), or, on the model, the position is here (indicating). That is the exact position. It is Oseliste, Donji Bukovci. They opened fire on the ambulance, and the physician who was in the ambulance, his name was Barbic, he died as a result of being wounded when the shooting took place, whereas the ambulance itself was kept in Bukovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who opened fire on the ambulance with the doctor inside?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was the crew at the checkpoint in Bukovci and Oseliste, the members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The doctor died. The vehicle was kept, they kept the ambulance, and any evacuation was rendered impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At one particular moment, you received information that the Grubesic family, they were parents of one of the HVO commanders, elderly folk, that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We received information that day that the Grubesic family had been killed. They were 65 years of age, and they were from Nezirovici. The information also said that another family had been killed from Besici, and that there was another -- that the attack was still being launched on a group of Croats who had been blocked and trapped between the villages of Nezirovici and Besici and the Oseliste village (indicating). In this area, all the Croats belonging to the Kacuni local commune found themselves in an encirclement and under a blockade by the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On that particular day, you gathered some volunteers, about 120 of them, and you started moving towards the obstacles set up by the BH army, the blockade from the direction of Kiseljak. Can you tell us what happened and how events were to develop and what happened to that group of people under your command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At about 3.30 p.m., we managed to collect about 120 volunteers from the Kiseljak municipality, and we started out from Kiseljak with six motor vehicles. We took the road, main road, across Gromiljak, Brestovsko, and Bilalovac, and stopped at the Plin Klokoti factory, and then went on on foot towards the barricade at Donji Bukovci with the intention of lifting the barricade and evacuating the civilians and the wounded from the Oseliste area. We started out on foot from Klokot using this road towards a feature on the map termed Gracac. It is feature 594. At about 4.30 p.m. or 4.40 p.m., we arrived at the positions of the BH army and we heard them talking at the Gracac feature as we approached, and I remember them saying that they were expecting a shift to replace them at about 5.00 p.m. There was an uncontrolled burst of gunfire. We were 30 to 50 metres away from each other. The consequences of that burst of gunfire on the HVO side and the group of men who were with me was that one man was killed and two to three soldiers were injured. I don't know the figures for the casualties on the BH army side, whether anybody was lightly wounded or not, because I saw that the positions at Gracac, that particular feature, had been left empty, void, after that conflict at the Gracac feature. The soldiers of the BH army had withdrawn in the direction of the village of Bukovci, Gracac, Bukovci, here (indicating), which enabled the villagers from Oseliste to move towards Jelenov Gaj, the gasworks there and, with my group of volunteers, returned to the Plin or gas factory called Klokoti. Having left Mato Lucic to be in charge, in the course of the night, of the displaced persons, I returned to Kiseljak with the vehicles and with the volunteers, and the volunteers went home for the night. They were, for the most part, people who lived in the Kiseljak local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This brings us to the 30th of January, 1993. Can you tell us whether, on that particular day, you launched an operation of any kind to try to protect some of the Muslim families in Kiseljak? What happened?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 30th of January, sometime in the morning, it was about 6.15 a.m., I received an invitation from the Brestovsko local community, Dugo Polje is indicated on the model, marked on the model, they said that they had noticed a mass of civilians going from Bilalovac and the surrounding villages and moving towards Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were the Croats from Bilalovac, and up until then, up until the 29th or 30th of January, there had been no conflicts or incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean in Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, no incidents in Bilalovac up until that time. They were arriving at the barracks in Kiseljak. There were a lot of high emotions. They were desperate at having been expelled and threatened, that they would undertake the same measures towards the Bosniak Muslims in the town of Kiseljak, the same kind of measures that the BH army undertook vis-à-vis them in the Bilalovac local community, so emotions were running high. In the course of the night between the 29th and 30th of January, they were expelled from the Bilalovac local community by the BH army forces. I asked the deputy commander of the police station in Kiseljak to ensure safety for the prominent Muslim citizens, that threats had been made --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "prominent Muslim families," do you mean prominent in terms of culture, religion, or did you mean the families of the political and military leaders of Muslims in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I meant the families of the political and military leaders from Kiseljak, from amongst the Bosniak Muslims, and also the families of the commanders of the police station in Kiseljak, and he was a Bosniak Muslim, so both the police, military, and political prominent Bosniak Muslims who had been threatened publicly by the expelled Croats from Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened in actual fact? Did the police listen to this request made by you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a patrol was designated, and it was there to supervise the vicinity around the houses or apartments of these families, and later on, I think the officers themselves came to learn of this, such as the chief of the police station, Ganija, and the deputy chief, Bujic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should now like to show a videotape, and I should like to ask our technical booth to dim the lights and start up the video. It is a very short video. I think that the booths have been given a copy. This is for the English. Just one moment so that the English booth can receive a copy of the text. This is a videotape which I received from Television Kiseljak of the day. It was taken after the events in the sports hall of the school in Kiseljak, which is where the refugees from Gusti Grab and Oseliste were located, precisely the event that you spoke about a moment ago. No sound yet. May we have the sound, please, sound track? We seem to be having some technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you prefer to continue or what would you like to do now, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just to see if the technical booth is ready. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voice-over) "They shot at us from all sides --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you rewind it back to the beginning, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voice-over) "A young man named Cavara Dalibor, and he is now going to tell us of his vision of the past events. Go ahead, Dalibor. "Well, I come from Gusti Grab. We fought, and they shot at us from Lugovi and from the other side, from Silos, where there are a number of villages. We did the best we could. They attacked us, and they came from outside, they were the people from Krajina and the Mujahedeen, and we had to withdraw because there were some wounded young men. While we were busy taking out the wounded young men, they entered our trenches, and we had to withdraw, and we went back behind the lines, and then they sent us out of that position and shot at us from all sides, both from Silos and from Lugovi, and we had to withdraw slowly. "The line had been drawn up until Jelenov Gaj, and then we went back on the lines. They attacked us again, and we found ourselves at Sirovi Panj. There were eight of us there who fought, and I think that there were at least 500 of them attacking us. We managed to refute the attack. One of our men was wounded, and that is how we managed to retain the line. It had not fallen yet. And when more of them came and they began grouping forces, they launched an onslaught of us, and we had to withdraw from Brestovsko, but I would like to tell them that we're going to return and that there will be no more Muslims in Busovaca. So much from me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This was shown on Television Kiseljak, and had you seen the tape at the time or is this the first time that you're looking at the tape?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I see the video for the first time, but what this witness is talking about is all known to me. I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is a young man of no more than 17, and let me just repeat his last comment, and tell me if this is something that you heard from others as well. "Still, I am giving them a message, that we will return and that Muslims will no longer survive in Busovaca. That's all I have to say." How do you comment on this vengeful remark by this young man?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is certainly a consequence of everything that this young man went through in this conflict, and this remark was made several days after he was expelled, and it reflected the feelings of the Croats in the local communes of Kacuni and Bilalovac. These feelings were shared there, and this further complicated our situation in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to the problems with these refugees who were upset and enraged and who were asking for revenge in Kiseljak, were there also problems in the organisation of the Ban Josip Jelisic Brigade? Was this a new, sudden, and unexpected situation, and how were you going about solving it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a major problem, because if you consider that the forces from Kiseljak, for the most part, were engaged at the front against the army of the Republika Srpska at Kokoska, Kobiljaca, the Pljesevac feature, and that part of the forces from Kiseljak, from the local communes of Brestovsko and Bilalovac, was already deployed at the Travnik front in the Paklarevo sector, also against the army of the Republika Srpska, then we were in the situation on that morning of the 30th of January to use the elderly men from the local commune of Brestovsko to establish the new front lines which were now against the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were facing the Brestovsko local commune and the rest of the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just remind the Judges, where were the young men from Brestovsko and Bilalovac at the time when you had to use the elderly men?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Two hundred young men were used in sector 1, which is called Paklarevo, in defence of the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that a number of refugees were upset and angry. I will now show you a document which you drafted, which is document D350, and I would also like the videotape to be marked for identification, a defence number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D543.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the videotape is D543. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now go back to document D350 which you drafted on the 31st of January, 1993 and sent to Mustafa Agic. Who was he? What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: A Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This was dated 31 January, 1993 to the attention of Mr. Mustafa Agic, and the reference is "Apology for the brutal behaviour of extremist member of the HVO in Kiseljak." "Dear sir, I have been informed by the competent authorities about the destructive behaviour of an uncontrolled group of HVO soldiers who demolished your catering establishment between 1400 and 1600 hours on 29 January, 1993. "I am aware of the fact that this kind of behaviour among the extremist element in the HVO undermines the security situation and creates mistrust among the inhabitants of Kiseljak who are concerned about their personal safety. However, I promise you that appropriate measures will be taken against the perpetrators of these acts. "I wish to apologise to you once again for everything that was done by the extremists in the ranks of the HVO. "Regards, Commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic." Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, in a situation where Croatians are being expelled, their houses are being burned down, we saw that the Croats in Dusina were massacred, what were your motives for apologising personally, as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, to a private businessman, a restaurant owner? What did you want to do by that? What were your motives?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The motives are perfectly clear from this document. I wanted to maintain good relations and to stabilise the situation in the Kiseljak area, and when I say "good relations," I mean the relations between the Croats and Bosniak Muslims in the area of the Kiseljak municipality. This was an incident, and I know that the incident was handled by the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the stamp, and can you tell me, whose stamp is this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the Ban Josip Jelacic HVO Brigade in Kiseljak, of their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why did you use a brigade stamp, being a commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I did not have another stamp, and the document gains more weight, so to speak, if it is also stamped in addition to being signed, and I used the only one that I had available to me at that time, which was the one of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have your back-up command post and office in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, I had no office there, and if I stayed in the barracks, I used the brigade commander's office. I did not have a separate office or a command post in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the January conflict and after that time, that is, throughout your stay in Kiseljak, and we will see that you stayed there all the way until early March, were any Muslim villages in the Kiseljak municipality attacked or disarmed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, no village was attacked or disarmed, not a single Muslim village or even hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were civilians arrested in Kiseljak during your stay there in January and February 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did any Muslim forcibly dig trenches in the Kiseljak municipality while you stayed there in January and February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, not a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was a single Muslim house burned down in the Kiseljak municipality while you stayed there in January and February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Not a single structure owned by the Bosniak Muslims was burned down or damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move on to the joint commission and overcoming the consequences of the conflict with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you tell me: What gains did the BH army achieve out of this conflict and what losses did the HVO incur?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: With the permission of Their Honours, I would like to point to the map. Could I get up and point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with this operation, created a corridor which includes Kacuni-Bilalovac on the main road between Kiseljak and Busovaca, and in this way it created a land link between the 3rd Corps in Zenica with the forces of the 4th Corps in Mostar and with part of the forces of the 1st Corps of the operative group named Igman, and in the territory of three municipalities, that is, Zenica, including the villages of Lasva, Dusina, and Visnjica conducted ethnic cleansing and expulsion of Croats from these villages; from the area of the Kacuni local commune, Croats were also ethnically cleansed from the villages of Nezirovici, Besici, Gusti Grab, Oseliste, Prosje, and partly the village of Bilalovac; and from the area of the Bilalovac local commune, Croats were expelled from the villages of Prviste, Odrace, Devetaci, Badnje, Milodraz, Sehitluci, and hamlets of the Bilalovac local commune in the area towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Approximately how many Croats were ethnically cleansed and driven in the direction of Kiseljak and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Around 2.100 Croats, and perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the first ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia carried out by any side?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the first ethnic cleansing in the three municipalities, that is, Zenica, Busovaca, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the first time that an army came to a village, killed the villagers, took prisoners of war, and burned down the village?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This new military situation -- and let's put aside the ethnic cleansing right now and what that meant for the inter-ethnic relations, that is, between Croats and Muslims -- what was the military situation of the HVO following this operation by the BH army or the situation of your Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we can look at it in two ways: First of all, the Operative Zone, with its headquarters in Vitez, remained without a communication line with the main staff in Mostar, and that was a huge strategic loss for the Operative Zone command. Secondly, we ended up with enclaves, so that Vitez, Busovaca, Zenica, Travnik, and Novi Travnik (indicating) comprised one enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which could be called Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Lasva Valley. And the other enclave was Kiseljak, Kresevo and, later on, Fojnica was also physically separated from Kiseljak and Kresevo, but on the 30th of January, 1993, Fojnica had communication line with Kiseljak but -- Kakanj also became an enclave. Sorry, let me show it on the map. For the Kiseljak HVO, Kakanj also became an enclave and Vares (indicating). In the north, on the main road Zenica-Zepce, would be where the next enclave was, that is, the Zepce enclave, so that is where the -- that was Zavidovici and Maglaj. Another additional enclave was Usora.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So if I understood well and I counted correctly, your Operative Zone was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where is Usora? I'm sorry. Where is that located? The last one you mentioned, where is that located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm missing my map because that's where I see it better, apart from the excellent photographs, of course, submitted by Mr. Hayman. But in the meantime, we have the maps here. So where is Usora again, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the town of Tesanj, which is due north from Zenica, and Usora is then due east from Tesanj (indicating). There is no town of Usora, there is only a Usora river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. So I understand there are five enclaves, if I understand correctly, Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that as -- I didn't mention Sarajevo as an enclave, but it was not as a consequence of this conflict, so Sarajevo could be added as a fourth operative group within the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So if we count Sarajevo, then your Operative Zone would have been broken up into six enclaves?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm pointing to Usora now (indicating). This is within the municipality -- in the territory of the municipalities of Doboj and Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But formally speaking, you remained the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone which would now include all six enclaves?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, you have six enclaves. In the circumstances of the structure or organisation which you had, which is the initial stages of transformation of the armed people into an army and in the conditions of the communication lines such as you had, what was your ability to command and control in real time and space with these enclaves which you had available?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I had no ability to command and control in real time in these six enclaves with the exception of the Kiseljak enclave which is where I stayed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay. Having sketched this military situation, let's move on to February. Throughout the month of February, you were in Kiseljak. Could you briefly and chronologically describe the main developments and your activities because at this time you were away from your main headquarters. Just give us a quick overview of this period, that is, following the first conflict in late January of 1993 and leading up to the second conflict in April. So let's start with the 1st of February, '93.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of January, 1993, due to the clear failure to implement the agreement which we had reached with the 3rd Corps on the 27th of January, I asked for a new meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps through the UN headquarters, and on the 1st of February, we held a new meeting. If I recall correctly, it was held in Vitez. General Morillon presided in this meeting, and the chief of the monitors, Mr. Flemming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we go to the meeting and what took place, can you just tell me what did the 3rd Corps fail to implement, what basic provision of the agreement of the 27th of January?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was cease-fire and the cessation of all hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we say that after the 27th of January, the worst violence and the most gains took place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These villages were attacked after the 27th, that is, the villages in the -- the villages in Kacuni and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, you went to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you describe how your trip went and what orders you gave to Mijo Bozic just before leaving Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that Kiseljak was filled with refugees who were very frustrated and, unfortunately, some of them were also armed, and I demanded of Commander Bozic to take all necessary steps and prevent any type of retaliation against the Bosniak Muslims in the town of Kiseljak and to remove the armed groups from Kiseljak and send them to the front lines, either one or the other side who were in the area of Kiseljak. I also asked to find collective accommodations for all refugees as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With whom, how, in what way did you start to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I received a notice to wait for the UNPROFOR vehicles and to use the armoured vehicles to go from the Kiseljak barracks to Vitez. I could not follow very well and observe the area as we passed, but I believe that we went towards Visoko, Kakanj, Zenica, and then to Vitez to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In other words, you did not use the short route, which is where the line of defence was, but you used the circuitous route?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It took us about 45 minutes to get there, which is what made me conclude that we had used this really circuitous route because there were only two communications lines open.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This circuitous route was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was under the full control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why were you not able to see where you were going? What stopped you? What prevented you from seeing this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only suppose that for security reasons, it was decided to put the blinds down on the armoured UN vehicles, and we were practically hermetically sealed within the armoured vehicles themselves and were not able to look out and see anything from within.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You reached the UN base in Vitez. Tell us who was at the meeting and what was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by the commander of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Morillon, and the head of the UN Monitoring Mission, Mr. Flemming. Also present at the meeting were Enver, the commander of the 3rd Corps, and Kadir Jusic, who represented the 3rd Corps of the BH army, and Dzemo, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You're referring to Dzemo Merdan, are you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dzemo Merdan, that's correct. I myself was present, and the head of the staff, Franjo Nakic, of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good time to clear up a terminological matter. The name of the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, his name was Dzemail Merdan, and "Dzemo" was short for "Dzemail"; is that correct? People who knew him better, they referred to him as "Dzemo." So is "Dzemo" an abbreviation of his full name, which was "Dzemail"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I knew him as Dzemo at that time, and Enver, and we communicated using that name at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General Morillon presided over the meeting. What did he say by way of introduction? How did he open the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In his introductory speech, he said that activities were under way in Geneva to come by a peaceful solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina and that he was surprised that the destruction that had taken place in the zone of the 3rd Corps of the BH army and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone had been expanded, and he asked that in the discussions to follow, Enver and myself should present our proposals as to how to stop this destruction. General Morillon took note of the fact that Croats had been expelled from Bilalovac, and after that, he emphasised that it was our task, and probably he had in mind mine and Enver's task, to build up mutual trust and confidence, to appoint liaison officers with the UN, and to establish PTT links and communications, that is to say, telegraph and telephone communication lines. When I was given the floor at the meeting, I emphasised in particular the fact that it was necessary to monitor and examine the way in which links were being relayed because, quite obviously, there had been some disturbances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You're talking about the telephone cables, are you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean cables as well, because in Bosnia, there were two forms of communications: cable links, telephone cable links, and radio relay transmitters, and it was enough for one of the relays to be upset for the link not to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the representatives of the International Community insisted that these communications be repaired and put right and re-established, did they have in mind the links between the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They had in mind overall communications, both civilian and military communications, which would enable the speedy settlement of mutual misunderstandings in the aim of achieving peace and a return of trust and confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue. What else was concluded at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I also put forward a number of suggestions at the meeting and said that we ought to intensify the work of the joint commission and that our deputies should be appointed and designated, so on the one hand, we had Nakic and, on the other side, Dzemo Merdan. I also asked for freedom of movement along the roads in our zone of responsibility, principally the road from Vitez-Kiseljak, Vitez-Zenica, and the other roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Another terminological qualification now, please. Franjo Nakic, what was his position in your command? What function and duty did he have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
